title: Read Nutrition Labels Fast
summary: A practical way to scan food labels without getting lost in every number or letting packaging claims make the decision for you.

steps.heading: Start with serving size
steps.body: The serving size tells you what amount the label numbers are based on. It is not a recommendation for how much you should eat. It is a reference point. If you eat two servings, the calories and nutrients are roughly doubled.

steps.heading: Calories are context, not a verdict
steps.body: Calories tell you how much energy is in a serving. They can be useful for awareness, but they do not tell the whole story. A food can be higher in calories and still be nutritious, filling, or worth including. Use the number as context, not as a moral score.

steps.heading: Scan nutrients to limit
steps.body: The FDA highlights saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars as nutrients many people may want to limit. A quick scan can help you compare products. This does not mean you must avoid every food with these nutrients. It means you can spot patterns and make more informed choices.

steps.heading: Look for nutrients to get more of
steps.body: Fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium are examples of nutrients many people may benefit from getting enough of. The percent Daily Value can help: 5% DV or less is considered low, while 20% DV or more is considered high.

steps.heading: Compare similar foods
steps.body: Labels are most useful when comparing similar products: two yogurts, two cereals, two frozen meals. Check that serving sizes are similar, then compare the nutrients that matter most to you. This keeps label reading practical instead of overwhelming.

takeaway: Read labels in order: serving size, calories, nutrients to limit, nutrients to get more of, then compare similar foods. The goal is faster awareness, not perfection.
